The Rufous-bellied thrush (Turdus rufiventris) is a medium-sized passerine that reaches adulthood with a clear sexual size dimorphism; adult females attain a maximum body mass of 72.2 grams [Wwi = 72.2 grams], while males are slightly smaller with an ultimate wet weight of 66.8 grams [Wwi = 66.8 grams]. This difference in adult mass likely reflects distinct energetic demands associated with egg production in females. At hatching, the altricial nestlings are remarkably small, with neonatal body mass recorded at 5.3 grams [Wwb = 5.3 grams], a value typical of thrushes that produce multiple broods per season. The embryonic development proceeds within eggs incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C]; under these thermal conditions, hatching occurs after an incubation period of 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days], a duration consistent with the relatively short incubation spans reported for other Turdus species breeding in subtropical lowlands.

At the ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which approximates the species' active metabolic range, the nestling period is brief: the time from hatching to fledging is 11 days [tx = 11 days]. This accelerated fledging schedule may be an adaptation to reduce predation risk, as nests are frequently depredated in the understory habitats this thrush occupies. During the post-fledging phase, juveniles continue to receive parental provisioning for several weeks. Sexual maturation is a gradual process, and field studies indicate that puberty is attained at 33 days since birth [tp = 33 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The physiological changes associated with gonadal development during this period are accompanied by an increase in body mass as the birds approach adult dimensions.

First reproduction in Turdus rufiventris occurs comparatively late in the first year, with the time since birth at first brood recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days] when the environmental temperature is 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delayed onset of breeding, relative to the attainment of physical maturity, is thought to reflect the need for juveniles to acquire foraging skills and establish territories before investing in offspring. The reproductive strategy involves multiple nesting attempts within a single breeding season. In terms of fecundity, females typically lay a clutch of 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt], and they can produce up to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 3 clutches per year] under favorable conditions. This high annual reproductive output is characteristic of many Neotropical thrushes inhabiting seasonal environments.

Longevity records for this species indicate a maximum lifespan of 17.5 years [am = 17.5 years] in wild populations, a remarkable duration for a bird of its size when considered at the standard reference body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Such extended survival likely contributes to the species' demographic stability, as older individuals accumulate breeding experience and maintain high annual fecundity. The comparatively slow pace of life, featuring a long adult lifespan alongside a relatively high annual reproductive output, places the Rufous-bellied thrush in an interesting position along the slow-fast continuum of avian life-history strategies. Comparative data from other Turdus species suggest that this combination of traits is particularly well-suited to environments with moderate but predictable seasonal resource pulses.

The reproductive strategy of Turdus rufiventris is thus finely tuned to its thermal environment. Under the temperature regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic phase of this species, the maximum reproductive output is best appreciated through the decomposition of its components: females lay 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per nesting attempt] and can produce up to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 3 clutches per year], yielding a substantial annual production of 9 to 12 offspring per year. The nestlings, initially weighing just 5.3 grams [Wwb = 5.3 grams], experience a dramatic increase in mass during their first two weeks, largely fueled by the high-protein diet provided by both parents. The fledging period of 11 days [tx = 11 days] is notably short, allowing adults to begin subsequent nesting attempts rapidly at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This compressed developmental timeline, combined with the capacity for multiple broods, underpins the species' demographic resilience in the face of environmental variability across its range.
